claims.text: The HfNbTiVAl10 alloy has a hierarchical heterostructure.
A hybrid imaging-and-machine-learning framework can predict Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture-related behavior for HfNbTiVAl10.
The proposed framework can be at least 50% more efficient than established multiscale simulations.
The proposed framework can be 20% more accurate than established multiscale simulations.
The alloy contains coarse grains with embedded nanoscale secondary phases and interfaces.
EBSD and TEM can provide quantitative descriptors including grain-size distribution, secondary-phase dispersion, and interface density for model training.
Coarse grains and nanoscale secondary phases jointly control localized stress distribution and strain accommodation.
Localized stress distribution and strain accommodation govern elastic response, yielding, and fracture toughness in this alloy.
Nonlinear machine-learning analysis can learn complex correlations between measured microstructural features and mechanical properties.
The learned correlations can capture scale-bridging behavior associated with local strain hardening and interface debonding.
Replacing finite-element or atomistic calculations with the learned model will enable faster property prediction.
Prediction time will decrease by at least 50% relative to conventional simulation approaches.
Errors in predicted Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness will be reduced by approximately 20% relative to conventional simulations.
Predictions will fall within approximately ±10% of independent experimental measurements.
Existing multiscale simulation techniques are computationally intensive and poorly suited to rapid prediction cycles.
Unrepresentative or inaccurate microstructural data can cause overfitting and failure to capture rare but mechanically critical features.
Processing-induced microstructural anomalies absent from the training set can limit predictive performance.
Model uncertainty arises from dataset representativeness, measurement quality, training bias, and incomplete representation of scale-coupled phenomena.
